events.title: Transistor Invented
events.blurb: Three physicists at an American industrial research laboratory demonstrated a working point-contact transistor — a tiny semiconductor device made from germanium that could amplify electrical signals without the vacuum tubes, heat, and bulk then required. Within a decade the invention had reshaped electronics; within five decades, billions of its descendants would fit on a single silicon chip smaller than a fingernail.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1947 — John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Labs. They shared the 1956 Nobel. Shockley's later semiconductor company, though commercially a failure, seeded Silicon Valley through the departure of its "Traitorous Eight" founders of Fairchild Semiconductor.

events.title: Microsoft Founded
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore and his 22-year-old friend, working out of a cheap room in an Albuquerque motel, formally established a partnership to develop software for microcomputers. Their first product had been a BASIC interpreter for the Altair 8800, licensed to the kit's manufacturer. The contract paid royalties per machine sold. Within seven years they would own the personal-computer operating system industry.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1975 — Bill Gates and Paul Allen. Originally "Micro-Soft." They moved to the Seattle suburb of Bellevue in 1979 and to Redmond in 1986. Allen left the company in 1983 after being diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma; he recovered, founded other businesses, died in 2018.

events.title: Apple Computer Founded
events.blurb: Two 20-something Californians, a college dropout and a self-taught engineer, formed a partnership to sell a printed-circuit-board computer design the engineer had developed and the dropout had realized was marketable. A third partner, older and more cautious, asked out within two weeks and sold his share back for $800. The initial product was a hand-built board requiring the buyer to supply their own power supply, keyboard, and case.
events.revealBlurb: April 1, 1976 — Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne. Wayne's 10 percent share would today be worth over $300 billion. He has said he doesn't regret selling out; he'd been in a startup before and wanted to avoid another personal-liability exposure.

events.title: IBM PC Released
events.blurb: The world's dominant mainframe computer maker released a small desktop machine built, unusually for the company, from off-the-shelf parts — an Intel 8088 processor, an operating system licensed from Microsoft, components any competitor could buy. Business customers trusted the name and bought millions. The design's open specifications led to a decade of "IBM compatible" clones that collectively made the Intel/Microsoft duopoly inevitable.
events.revealBlurb: August 12, 1981 — IBM PC model 5150. It had 16KB of RAM and no hard drive. IBM's decision to source DOS from Microsoft, rather than write it in-house, is usually cited as the great strategic error of 20th-century computing. Gates retained all distribution rights.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: 13th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: The first of three Reconstruction-era amendments was ratified eight months after a brutal civil war ended, abolishing slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States except as punishment for crime. The exception clause would become the legal scaffolding for convict-leasing systems that reproduced plantation labor for another 80 years.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1865 — when Georgia became the 27th state to ratify. Mississippi officially ratified only in 1995, and didn't certify it until 2013, due to a paperwork oversight.

events.title: 14th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: Ratified in the aftermath of civil war, a constitutional amendment granted citizenship to "all persons born or naturalized in the United States," promised them equal protection under the laws, and guaranteed due process. Its sweeping language became, a century later, the foundation of Supreme Court rulings on school segregation, interracial marriage, abortion, and marriage equality.
events.revealBlurb: July 9, 1868 — citizenship via birthright. Its authors were thinking of formerly enslaved people; its practical effect reshaped virtually every area of American law. The "equal protection clause" alone has been cited in over 400 Supreme Court cases.

events.title: Military Desegregation Order
events.blurb: A U.S. president signed an executive order mandating "equality of treatment and opportunity" in the armed forces without regard to race, color, religion, or national origin. The army resisted for nearly five years; full integration of combat units was not achieved until the Korean War made ignoring Black replacements impossible.
events.revealBlurb: July 26, 1948 — Executive Order 9981, Harry Truman. He signed it partly out of conviction, partly because Black voters in northern cities were now pivotal to Democratic victory. The last all-Black unit was dissolved in 1954.

events.title: Birmingham Children's Crusade
events.blurb: Over several days in a notoriously segregated Alabama steel city, more than a thousand Black schoolchildren — some as young as 6 — marched out of classes in organized protest. Police commissioner Bull Connor ordered fire hoses and attack dogs deployed against them. Photographs of a teenage boy lunged at by a German shepherd appeared on front pages across the world.
events.revealBlurb: May 2-5, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. King agreed to use children over the objections of many advisers; they were less vulnerable to losing jobs for protesting. Within weeks, the Kennedy administration introduced what became the Civil Rights Act.

events.title: Martin Luther King Jr. Assassinated
events.blurb: Stepping onto the balcony outside Room 306 of a Tennessee motel where he was staying while supporting a sanitation workers' strike, the country's most prominent civil rights leader was shot once with a high-powered rifle from across the street. He died an hour later at a nearby hospital. He was 39. Riots broke out in more than 100 American cities within hours of the news.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1968 — Lorraine Motel, Memphis. His killer, escaped convict James Earl Ray, was captured in London two months later. The night before, King had ended a speech with: "I've been to the mountaintop. I may not get there with you, but we, as a people, will get to the Promised Land."

events.title: Turing's Computable Numbers
events.blurb: A 23-year-old British mathematician submitted a paper describing a hypothetical abstract machine — an infinite tape with a movable read/write head obeying a simple finite rule table — that could in principle compute anything a human mathematician could work out by following a procedure. The paper was intended to settle a famous open problem in formal logic; along the way it laid the mathematical groundwork for general-purpose computing.
events.revealBlurb: 1936 — Alan Turing, "On Computable Numbers." Written while he was a 23-year-old student. Turing worked with a physical analogue of the machine at Bletchley Park during WWII to break German Enigma ciphers. He was chemically castrated for homosexuality and died in 1954, probably by suicide.

events.title: ENIAC Unveiled
events.blurb: Engineers at an American university publicly demonstrated an 27-tonne general-purpose electronic computer, filling a 30 by 15 metre room with 17,468 vacuum tubes, 10,000 capacitors, and 6,000 switches. The machine calculated artillery-shell trajectories 2,400 times faster than a human with an adding machine. Programming it required physically rewiring hundreds of cables; the programmers — all women — had to crawl inside to swap plugs.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1946 — University of Pennsylvania. Designers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly. Programmers: Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas, and Ruth Lichterman. They were not invited to the unveiling dinner; their faces were cropped out of celebratory photos for decades.

events.title: First Cellular Phone Call
events.blurb: A Motorola engineer, standing on a Manhattan street with a 1.1-kilogram "brick" prototype handset to his ear, placed a phone call to his chief rival at a competing company's research lab — and made sure to inform him what he was doing. The handset's battery gave 35 minutes of talk time after 10 hours of charging. Motorola would spend another decade getting a lighter version to market.
events.revealBlurb: April 3, 1973 — Martin Cooper of Motorola called Joel Engel at Bell Labs. The prototype was the DynaTAC 8000x. It sold commercially in 1983 for $3,995. Cooper later said he'd been inspired by the communicator in Star Trek.

events.title: First Android Phone Released
events.blurb: A Taiwanese handset maker released the first commercial phone running an open-source mobile operating system developed by a Silicon Valley search-engine company, available through a US mobile carrier. The device had a physical keyboard that slid out from under the screen; unlike the rival iPhone, users could install apps from anywhere, replace the default apps, and generally modify the device at will. Open-ecosystem Android would grow to dominate global smartphone market share.
events.revealBlurb: October 22, 2008 — T-Mobile G1 (HTC Dream), running Android 1.0. Google had quietly acquired Android Inc. for $50 million in 2005. By 2013 more than half of smartphones sold ran Android; today it's over 70 percent globally.

events.title: iPad Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company released a 9.7-inch tablet — something between a smartphone and a laptop — running the same operating system as its phone. The product's name had been mocked in advance for rhyming with certain feminine-hygiene products; the device itself went on to redefine a computing form factor that previous attempts by Microsoft and others had never managed to make stick. It sold 3 million units in its first 80 days.
events.revealBlurb: April 3, 2010 — Apple iPad. Steve Jobs' last major product launch. "I think we have a winner here," he said at the introduction. Microsoft's Bill Gates had been pushing tablet PCs for a decade; Apple's combination of software, battery, and price finally made the form factor work.

events.title: Justinian's Code Issued
events.blurb: A Byzantine emperor's commission of ten jurists, working for 14 months, compiled nearly a thousand years of Roman legal rulings into a single four-part code. It became the foundation of civil-law systems across continental Europe and, centuries later, Latin America. Imperial-era laws contradicted themselves; the code resolved the contradictions by fiat.
events.revealBlurb: April 7, 529 — Emperor Justinian I issued the first edition. The final compilation, called the Corpus Juris Civilis, influenced the Napoleonic Code and every legal system modeled on it. Law students still read excerpts today.

events.title: First Crusade Takes Jerusalem
events.blurb: After a month-long siege and a three-year, 3,000-kilometre march from Europe, an army of Frankish knights and footsoldiers breached the walls of a holy city in the Levant and slaughtered its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants indiscriminately over two days — perhaps 30,000 people. The first crusader state was established with a European dynasty on the throne; it would last 88 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1099 — the siege was broken when two Flemish knights scaled a siege tower onto the wall. The leaders competed to be the first to reach the Holy Sepulchre. Godfrey of Bouillon refused the crown of a city "where his savior had worn a crown of thorns" — he was titled "Defender" instead.

events.title: Magna Carta Sealed
events.blurb: Facing armed revolt by his barons after a series of disastrous foreign wars and arbitrary taxation, an English king met them in a meadow beside the Thames and affixed his seal to a 63-clause charter limiting royal power, guaranteeing trial by peers, and making free men subject only to "the law of the land." He repudiated it within ten weeks; civil war resumed.
events.revealBlurb: June 15, 1215 — King John at Runnymede. Only three original copies survive. Clauses against arbitrary imprisonment echo today through American due-process law. The barons were self-interested, not democratic, but the language was universal enough to outlive them.

events.title: Battle of Legnica
events.blurb: A Mongol detachment under a grandson of Genghis Khan annihilated a combined Polish, Silesian, and Templar army in a field southwest of a town in Lower Silesia, killing a duke and most of his knights. The defeat should have opened central Europe to full Mongol conquest. Instead, news reached the army that the Great Khan in distant Karakorum had died, and the generals withdrew to attend the succession.
events.revealBlurb: April 9, 1241 — Mongol commander Orda. The Mongols traditionally displayed the severed right ears of the dead to count the slain; sources claim they filled nine large sacks. Europe was saved by Mongol electoral politics, not European arms.

events.title: Battle of Agincourt
events.blurb: An exhausted English army, heavily outnumbered, caught in thick mud on a narrow front between two woods in northern France, stood behind sharpened wooden stakes and cut down the armored flower of French nobility with longbows at point-blank range. The French dead included a constable, three dukes, and over 1,500 knights; English losses were perhaps 400. Shakespeare would turn it into a speech 180 years later.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1415 — Henry V on St. Crispin's Day. Henry ordered the slaughter of prisoners mid-battle when he feared a rear attack; this remains controversial. The longbow's armor-piercing arrowheads were called "bodkins."

events.title: Tylenol Murders
events.blurb: Seven people in the Chicago area died after taking over-the-counter acetaminophen capsules that had been laced with potassium cyanide by an unknown tamperer. The crisis triggered a nationwide recall of 31 million bottles, launched the tamper-resistant packaging industry, and reshaped pharmaceutical manufacturing standards permanently. Johnson & Johnson's swift and transparent response became a classic case study in crisis management. The killer was never identified.
events.revealBlurb: September 29-October 1, 1982 — seven deaths in Chicago suburbs. Pills had been purchased, tampered with, and returned to drugstore shelves. James William Lewis, a former suspect, died in 2023 maintaining his innocence. Tamper-proof packaging became a federal mandate within six months.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: Madonna's "Like a Prayer" Video
events.blurb: The music video for a 30-year-old singer's new single, featuring burning crosses, stigmata, and the singer kissing a Black saint statue coming to life, premiered during a Pepsi commercial at the start of a television special paid for by the soft-drink company. The Vatican condemned the video as blasphemous; conservative Christian groups organized boycotts; Pepsi paid the singer $5 million to sever their sponsorship deal. Her album sold 15 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1989 — the Pepsi commercial; the full video premiered on MTV March 3. Director Mary Lambert. The controversy gave Madonna an estimated $5 million for the Pepsi deal plus enormous free publicity; she kept the money. The album "Like a Prayer" remains her best-reviewed.

events.title: Seinfeld Premieres
events.blurb: A 90-minute pilot episode titled "The Seinfeld Chronicles" aired on NBC, starring a 35-year-old New York stand-up comedian as a fictionalized version of himself and three friends navigating petty social minutiae in Manhattan. NBC had almost dropped the show; test audiences had responded coolly. A show famously about "nothing," it would run 180 episodes over nine seasons and become one of the most influential sitcoms in television history.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1989 — Jerry Seinfeld, Jason Alexander, Michael Richards (Julia Louis-Dreyfus joined season 2). Co-creator Larry David later made Curb Your Enthusiasm, essentially a Seinfeld-universe spinoff. The cast famously turned down $5 million per episode each to continue past season 9.

events.title: Kurt Cobain Dies
events.blurb: A 27-year-old grunge-rock frontman was found dead of a self-inflicted shotgun wound in the greenhouse above the garage of his Seattle home. He had struggled with heroin addiction, a collapsed marriage, chronic stomach pain, and the deep anxieties of sudden fame. His suicide note quoted a line from a Neil Young song: "It's better to burn out than to fade away." A public memorial at Seattle Center drew 7,000 mourners.
events.revealBlurb: April 5, 1994 — Kurt Cobain of Nirvana. The body was not discovered for three days, by an electrician installing a security system. Conspiracy theories have persisted for decades. Cobain joined the "27 Club" of pop musicians who died at that age, including Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, Jim Morrison, and Amy Winehouse.

events.title: First Ancient Olympic Games
events.blurb: A religious festival held every four years in honour of Zeus at a sacred grove in the western Peloponnese began with a single footrace — a sprint of about 192 metres — won by a cook from the nearby city of Elis. Over subsequent centuries, the games expanded to include additional running events, wrestling, boxing, pankration, pentathlon, and chariot racing. The festival ran continuously for nearly 1,200 years before a Christian emperor banned it.
events.revealBlurb: 776 BCE — traditional date of first games at Olympia; winner Coroebus of Elis. The festival was abolished by Emperor Theodosius I in 393 CE as part of his suppression of pagan rites. It was revived as the modern Olympics in Athens, 1896.

events.title: First Modern Olympics
events.blurb: The first modern Summer Olympic Games opened in an Athens marble stadium built on the foundations of a Panathenaic-festival venue 1,500 years earlier. 241 athletes from 14 nations competed in 43 events over nine days. An amateur Greek water-carrier named Spiridon Louis won the marathon, run along the road from the town to the stadium, and became an instant national hero. A 27-year-old French baron had championed the revival for nearly a decade before the games.
events.revealBlurb: April 6, 1896 — the baron was Pierre de Coubertin. Louis won his race in 2:58:50 carrying a bouquet from his village; his prize included a year's worth of free meals and a plot of land. There were no women athletes; Coubertin considered female participation "impractical, uninteresting, and incorrect."

events.title: FIFA Founded
events.blurb: Representatives of seven European national football associations — Belgium, Denmark, France, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland — met at a Paris sports association's offices and established an international governing body for the sport. England, which had invented the modern codified game and considered itself the natural authority, declined to attend, joined in 1905, and withdrew multiple times over subsequent decades in petty disputes. The organization would run the World Cup from 1930 on.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1904 — Fédération Internationale de Football Association, Paris. Its first president was Robert Guérin. FIFA now has 211 member associations, more than the UN. Its headquarters moved to Zurich in 1932 and have been there since.

events.title: Hank Aaron Breaks Ruth's Record
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Atlanta outfielder hit his 715th career home run off a Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher, breaking Babe Ruth's 39-year-old career record in front of a sellout home crowd. He had endured a year of death threats, racist mail, and FBI protection as he approached the record. As he rounded second base, two white college students ran onto the field alongside him — security later decided they had meant only to escort him. He tipped his cap as he crossed home plate.
events.revealBlurb: April 8, 1974 — Hank Aaron at Atlanta-Fulton County Stadium, off Al Downing. His final career total was 755 home runs, which stood as the record until Barry Bonds passed it in 2007. The FBI had warned him that multiple credible plots to assassinate him were active that season.

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: Confederate Attack on Fort Sumter
events.blurb: At 4:30 in the morning, Confederate artillery opened fire on the federal garrison at Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, beginning a 34-hour bombardment that forced the Union to surrender and formally launched the deadliest war in American history. No one was killed in the bombardment itself — two Union soldiers died in a cannon accident during the surrender ceremony.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1861 — Charleston, South Carolina. The Confederacy fired over 4,000 shells at the fort; Union defenders fired roughly 1,000 back. Nobody died in combat during the entire engagement. Within four days, President Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers, and four more states seceded to join the Confederacy.

events.title: Abraham Lincoln Assassinated
events.blurb: At approximately 10:15 pm that night — five days after Confederate General Robert E. Lee surrendered at Appomattox — actor and Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln in the head at Ford's Theatre in Washington. Lincoln never regained consciousness and died at 7:22 the following morning; he was the first American president to be assassinated.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 1865 — Ford's Theatre, Washington, D.C. Booth coordinated simultaneous attacks on Vice President Johnson and Secretary of State Seward the same night; both failed. Lincoln's bodyguard had left his post to watch the play from a better vantage point.

events.title: Black Sunday: The Dust Bowl's Worst Storm
events.blurb: That spring Sunday, a wall of dust estimated at 500 to 600 feet high swept across the southern Great Plains at 60 miles per hour, blotting out the sun and turning a warm afternoon into absolute darkness across Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, and Colorado. The storm — the worst of dozens of black blizzards that had devastated the region since 1930 — was the event that gave the entire catastrophe its name: reporter Robert Geiger called the region "the Dust Bowl" the next day.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 1935 — Southern Great Plains. An estimated 300,000 tons of topsoil were displaced in a single afternoon. The Dust Bowl ultimately displaced approximately 3.5 million people from the Great Plains — the largest internal migration in American history to that point.

events.title: Apollo 1 Launchpad Fire
events.blurb: During a ground test at Cape Kennedy that afternoon, a fire broke out inside the Apollo 1 command module, killing all three crew members — Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee — in less than a minute. The cause was an electrical spark in an atmosphere of pure oxygen at elevated pressure, and the hatch could not be opened quickly enough to save anyone.
events.revealBlurb: January 27, 1967 — Launch Complex 34, Cape Kennedy, Florida. The crew could not escape because the hatch required 90 seconds to open inward — and the fire created pressure that made it impossible to swing. The disaster set the Moon program back 20 months but ultimately produced a safer spacecraft.

events.title: Bush v. Gore Halts Florida Recount
events.blurb: The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 to halt the manual recount of Florida's contested presidential ballots, effectively awarding the state's 25 electoral votes to Republican George W. Bush and deciding the closest presidential election since 1876. The margin in Florida's certified count was 537 votes out of nearly 6 million cast; Al Gore ultimately conceded, and Bush won the presidency 271–266 in the Electoral College.
events.revealBlurb: December 12, 2000 — Washington, D.C. The per curiam opinion included the extraordinary disclaimer that the ruling "is limited to the present circumstances" and should not be treated as precedent. The butterfly ballot design in Palm Beach County alone may have cost Gore 2,000–3,000 votes to Pat Buchanan.

events.title: First National Film Awards Ceremony
events.blurb: India's first government-adjudicated film awards were presented at Vigyan Bhavan in New Delhi by the President of the Republic, honouring the best films of 1953 across features, documentaries, and children's cinema. The ceremony established that Indian cinema was not merely entertainment but a matter of national cultural policy — a position that has shaped every film ministry since.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 1954. First Best Feature Film: Shyamchi Aai, a Marathi film about maternal devotion — not a Bombay product, a signal about the awards' intent to honour all Indian languages. The ceremony was conceived explicitly to reward what the state considered the right kind of cinema.

events.title: Guide Released
events.blurb: A tourist guide who becomes first the manager and then the lover of a classical dancer, before his imprisonment transforms him into a reluctant holy man, gave Dev Anand his most demanding role and Waheeda Rehman her finest screen hour. Shot simultaneously in Hindi and English for two different markets, only the Hindi version became a classic; the English cut disappeared quietly.
events.revealBlurb: April 2, 1965 (India) — directed by Vijay Anand, based on R.K. Narayan's 1960 Sahitya Akademi Award-winning novel The Guide. Narayan disliked the film adaptation. The English version, co-produced with a US studio, was screened briefly in America then shelved; a print was discovered decades later.

events.title: Sholay Released
events.blurb: A three-hour curry Western about two small-time criminals hired by a retired policeman to hunt a ruthless dacoit opened on India's Independence Day to a tepid first week before word-of-mouth turned it into the longest-running Indian film of all time. It played uninterrupted at a single Bombay theatre for five and a half years — 286 consecutive weeks.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1975. Director Ramesh Sippy. Amjad Khan as Gabbar Singh was nearly replaced because the scriptwriter thought his voice was too thin. The original ending showed Thakur killing Gabbar with spiked shoes — the censor board forced a reshoot. "Kitne aadmi the?" became a national catchphrase.

events.title: Slumdog Millionaire Wins Best Picture
events.blurb: A British-directed film set entirely in Mumbai — shot partly in the Dharavi slum with non-professional child actors, partly in the chaos of the city's streets — swept eight Oscars including Best Picture at the 81st Academy Awards, making it the first film primarily set and cast in India to win the top prize. Its pavement-to-riches structure was lifted directly from Bollywood's own playbook.
events.revealBlurb: February 22, 2009. Directed by Danny Boyle. A.R. Rahman won Best Original Score and Best Original Song for "Jai Ho" — his first Oscars, received in the same night. The child actors from the film were discovered to be living in poverty after production wrapped, triggering international headlines.

events.title: KGF: Chapter 2 Released
events.blurb: A Kannada-language action sequel about a gold miner's violent rise and rule over an illegal mining empire released simultaneously in five languages, broke the opening-day records of every film before it in the Hindi belt, and became the first Kannada film to gross ₹1,000 crore — a moment that announced South Indian cinema's claim on the pan-India blockbuster market.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 2022 — directed by Prashanth Neel. KGF Chapter 1 had been a slow-burn cult hit two years earlier; the sequel was designed from the outset as the louder, bigger answer. Yash, who plays Rocky, was a regional star of modest fame before Chapter 1; after Chapter 2 he turned down a reported 50 offers in a single week.

events.title: Archimedes' Principle of Buoyancy
events.blurb: A Greek mathematician established that an object submerged in fluid is buoyed upward by a force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces — a principle explaining why objects float or sink and allowing the density of irregular objects to be measured precisely. The insight reportedly struck the mathematician while stepping into a bath, causing him to run through the streets in excitement.
events.revealBlurb: c. 250 BCE — the "Eureka" bath story was first told by the Roman writer Vitruvius about 200 years after Archimedes lived, so historians treat it sceptically. What is not disputed is that Archimedes wrote it all down carefully in On Floating Bodies, one of the oldest surviving works of physics. He also calculated an approximation of pi accurate to three decimal places.

events.title: Copernican Heliocentric Model Published
events.blurb: A six-volume astronomical treatise placed the Sun rather than the Earth at the centre of the universe, arguing that Earth was just one of several planets orbiting the Sun and that Earth's own daily rotation explained the apparent motion of the stars. The author received the first printed copy on the day he died.
events.revealBlurb: 1543 — Copernicus sat on the manuscript for years, fearing ridicule. A colleague secretly arranged its publication; legend holds the author held the final printed pages on his deathbed. The Church placed the book on its Index of Forbidden Books 73 years after publication — once it actually started to threaten orthodoxy.

events.title: Continental Drift Hypothesis Presented
events.blurb: A German meteorologist proposed that Earth's continents were once joined in a single supercontinent that had since broken apart and drifted slowly across the ocean floor, citing the geometric fit of coastlines, matching fossil records on opposite sides of the Atlantic, and ancient glacial scour marks in tropical regions. The geological community's response was immediate and largely hostile.
events.revealBlurb: January 6, 1912 — Alfred Wegener's hypothesis was mocked at a major American geological meeting in 1926, where a speaker suggested geologists should "be instantly prepared to disregard" it. Wegener died on a Greenland expedition in 1930. The mechanism he was missing — seafloor spreading — was found by Harry Hess in the 1960s.

events.title: Human Genome Project Completed
events.blurb: An international consortium announced the completion of a map of the entire 3-billion-letter chemical sequence of human DNA, covering 99 percent of gene-containing regions at 99.99 percent accuracy — two years ahead of schedule. The project, begun in 1990, required coordinating laboratories across six countries and produced a reference sequence that has underpinned virtually every major advance in genetic medicine since.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 2003 — a rival private effort by Celera Genomics, led by Craig Venter, raced the public consortium and forced both teams to declare a joint "completion" in 2000. The actual finished sequence was only completed in 2003. A truly gapless human genome wasn't assembled until 2022, when long-read sequencing technology filled the remaining 8%.

events.title: First Black Hole Image Captured
events.blurb: A global network of radio telescopes, coordinated to act as a single Earth-sized dish, produced the first direct image of a black hole's event horizon — a glowing ring of superheated gas surrounding a dark central void at the centre of a galaxy 55 million light-years away. Processing the petabytes of data required a custom algorithm developed in part by a graduate student whose contribution went initially unrecognised.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 2019 — the black hole in galaxy M87 is 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun. Katie Bouman, then a postdoc, developed much of the imaging algorithm and became briefly internet-famous when a photo of her looking at the result on a laptop went viral. The press release was coordinated across six cities in six time zones simultaneously.

events.title: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
events.blurb: An English civil servant in his mid-fifties died leaving unfinished a collection of stories told by pilgrims riding from Southwark to a Kentish cathedral shrine. Written in Middle English rather than French or Latin, the work demonstrated the poetic range of the English vernacular across a social spectrum — knights, millers, cooks, pardoners, the famously bawdy Wife of Bath. Only 24 of a planned 120 tales were ever completed.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1400 — Geoffrey Chaucer. He is often called the father of English literature. Roughly 80 manuscripts survive; the earliest complete ones date from the 1410s. The Wife of Bath's Tale became an early feminist touchstone.

events.title: War and Peace Published
events.blurb: A 41-year-old Russian aristocrat completed the last serial installment of a vast historical novel following five aristocratic families through Russia's Napoleonic Wars. The finished work ran over 1,200 pages and combined personal drama, military history, and a 200-page essay on the philosophy of history tacked onto the end. The author rewrote the opening sentence at least seven times.
events.revealBlurb: 1869 — Leo Tolstoy. It was serialized in the journal Russky Vestnik between 1865 and 1869. Tolstoy later disowned most of his fiction on religious grounds and decades later attempted to destroy his own estate's copyright to prevent his heirs from profiting.

events.title: Rabindranath Tagore Wins Nobel
events.blurb: A 52-year-old Bengali polymath — poet, novelist, philosopher, composer, painter — was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the first non-European and the first Asian to receive the honour. The Swedish Academy specifically cited his English translation of his own Bengali poetry collection "Gitanjali." The award brought him international fame; at home in colonial India it cemented him as a national cultural figure.
events.revealBlurb: November 13, 1913 — Rabindranath Tagore. He renounced his British knighthood in 1919 after the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre. He composed the national anthems of both India ("Jana Gana Mana") and Bangladesh ("Amar Shonar Bangla"), two of three anthems he wrote for different countries.

events.title: The Great Gatsby Published
events.blurb: A 28-year-old American novelist published his third novel — a 218-page story about a wealthy bootlegger's obsessive love for an old flame now married to a brutish Yale football star, narrated by a Midwestern newcomer to Long Island. Reviews were respectable; sales were tepid. The author died 15 years later considering himself a failure. The book was rediscovered during WWII when Armed Services Editions shipped 155,000 copies to U.S. soldiers; it is now read in every American high school.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 1925 — F. Scott Fitzgerald. Original print run: 20,870 copies. Fitzgerald earned $200 in royalties from his fourth novel "Tender Is the Night." His high-schooler daughter Scottie, who detested "The Great Gatsby," left her father's papers to Princeton.

events.title: 1984 Published
events.blurb: A 46-year-old English novelist, suffering from advanced tuberculosis on a remote Scottish island, published a dystopian novel depicting a totalitarian state where history is continuously rewritten, all speech is monitored, and a figurehead leader is omnipresent. He had been working on it for four years; he typed much of it lying in bed. He died of the disease seven months later. The book gave English a vocabulary for surveillance authoritarianism that has never been matched.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 1949 — George Orwell (Eric Blair). Written on the island of Jura. "Big Brother," "doublethink," "thought police," "Newspeak," and "Orwellian" all entered English usage. The title's year was chosen by reversing 1948, the year he completed the draft.

events.title: Mount Tambora Eruption
events.blurb: A volcano on an Indonesian island blew its top in the most powerful eruption in recorded history, spewing 150 cubic kilometres of material into the atmosphere. The sulphate aerosols lingered in the stratosphere for years, cooling global temperatures by roughly a degree and producing crop failures, famine, and snow in June across the northern hemisphere the following year.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 1815 — Mount Tambora on Sumbawa, Indonesia. 1816 became "the year without a summer." Mary Shelley, trapped indoors by endless rain in Switzerland, wrote Frankenstein. J.M.W. Turner's lurid sunsets from the decade owe their color to Tambora's dust.

events.title: Mount Pelée Eruption
events.blurb: A volcanic mountain on a Caribbean island unleashed a pyroclastic flow — a superheated cloud of gas and ash travelling at hurricane speed — that swept down onto the colonial capital below and killed nearly every one of the town's 28,000 inhabitants in about 60 seconds. Two survivors were found: a shoemaker on the outskirts and a prisoner locked in a thick-walled dungeon.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1902 — Saint-Pierre, Martinique. The prisoner, Ludger Sylbaris, was saved by his stone cell, horribly burned but alive. He later joined Barnum & Bailey Circus as "the man who lived through Doomsday."

events.title: San Francisco Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake ripped a 477-kilometre tear through the fault running up the California coast, hitting a West Coast boom city just after 5 AM. The shaking was severe, but the four-day fire that followed — fed by broken gas mains and fought with limited water from shattered pipes — did most of the damage, destroying 80 percent of the city and killing around 3,000.
events.revealBlurb: April 18, 1906 — San Francisco. The mayor authorized dynamiting buildings to create firebreaks; most of the dynamiting actually spread the fire. The opera singer Enrico Caruso, in town for a performance, vowed never to return. He didn't.

events.title: Bhopal Disaster
events.blurb: A cloud of methyl isocyanate gas leaked from a pesticide plant on the outskirts of a central Indian city shortly after midnight, drifting over densely populated slums whose inhabitants woke choking and blind. Between 8,000 and 16,000 people died in the immediate aftermath; 500,000 were injured. Groundwater at the site remains contaminated four decades on.
events.revealBlurb: December 2-3, 1984 — Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. The plant was owned by Union Carbide; the American parent company settled for $470 million, a fraction of the actual cost. The CEO, Warren Anderson, was briefly arrested and then quietly released; India's extradition requests were ignored.

events.title: Hurricane Katrina
events.blurb: A Category 3 hurricane made landfall on the US Gulf Coast, driving a storm surge that overtopped and breached the levee system protecting a major port city lying largely below sea level. 80 percent of the city flooded; 1,392 people died. The chaotic federal response — images of thousands stranded on a sports stadium roof, bodies floating in water — inflicted lasting damage on the administration in power.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 2005 — New Orleans, Louisiana. The Superdome housed 30,000 evacuees for five days in deteriorating conditions. The head of FEMA, Michael Brown, had previously run the International Arabian Horse Association; he resigned within two weeks.

events.title: First Human in Orbit
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Soviet Air Force pilot rode a modified intercontinental ballistic missile into a single orbit reaching 327 km altitude, completing one lap of Earth in 108 minutes before ejecting from his capsule at 7 km and parachuting separately to a field in southern Russia. The mission was fully automated; Gagarin held an emergency manual-control key sealed in an envelope in case he needed it.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1961 — Vostok 1. Gagarin was chosen partly because he was 1.57 m tall and fit the cramped capsule. He shouted "Poyekhali!" ("Let's go!") at liftoff — the same casual phrase Russian pilots use to start any flight. The module didn't fully separate and sent him spinning at 8 Gs before a wire bundle burned through.

events.title: Apollo 13 Oxygen Tank Rupture
events.blurb: An oxygen tank in the Apollo 13 Service Module exploded 56 hours into the mission, venting both oxygen tanks to space and forcing the crew to abandon the Command Module for the Lunar Module, which was designed to support two people for two days but kept three alive for four. The crew looped around the Moon and returned safely after improvising a CO₂ scrubber from materials aboard using instructions radioed from Earth.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1970 — Apollo 13. The tank that exploded had been accidentally dropped during ground testing 18 months earlier. Mission controllers in Houston coined "successful failure" to describe the outcome. The crew consumed so little water during the return that all three were severely dehydrated; Lovell lost 6.5 kg.

events.title: First Space Station Launched
events.blurb: The Soviet Union placed the world's first space station, Salyut 1, into low Earth orbit using a Proton rocket. The 18.9-metre station provided a pressurized working volume of 90 cubic meters across three interconnected compartments and was designed to host rotating crews arriving by Soyuz capsule for extended scientific work.
events.revealBlurb: April 19, 1971 — Salyut 1. The station's only successful resident crew — Soyuz 11 — spent 23 days aboard, setting a spaceflight endurance record. All three died during reentry when a faulty valve vented the cabin to vacuum; they were found in their seats, un-suited. The disaster prompted a redesign requiring all cosmonauts to wear pressure suits during docking.

events.title: First American Woman in Space
events.blurb: Physicist Sally Ride flew aboard Space Shuttle Challenger as a mission specialist on STS-7, becoming the first American woman and the youngest American in space at 32. The six-day mission deployed two communications satellites and was the first shuttle flight to use a robotic arm to retrieve a free-flying satellite.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — STS-7. A reporter asked Ride before launch whether spaceflight would affect her reproductive organs; she deadpanned that no one had asked her male crewmates the same question. NASA engineers reportedly asked whether 100 tampons would be enough for the six-day flight "just to be safe." She flew again in 1984 and co-founded a science education company.

events.title: Curiosity Mars Rover Landing
events.blurb: NASA's Curiosity rover descended through the Martian atmosphere using a novel sky-crane system that lowered the 899 kg rover on nylon cables from a hovering rocket-powered platform before flying away and crashing at a safe distance. The rover landed in Gale Crater and confirmed within the first year that Mars once had liquid water capable of supporting microbial life.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 2012 — Mars Science Laboratory. Engineers called the entry sequence "seven minutes of terror" because Mars is 14 light-minutes away — by the time Earth received confirmation that the descent had begun, Curiosity was already alive or dead on the surface. The first wheel tracks Curiosity made on Mars spelled "JPL" in Morse code.

events.title: Handel's Messiah Premieres
events.blurb: A 57-year-old German-born, London-resident composer conducted the premiere of a three-hour oratorio he had written in 24 days, at a charity concert in a hall in an Irish capital. Ladies were asked not to wear hoops and gentlemen not to wear swords so more could fit in the venue. The proceeds benefited a hospital, a prison society, and a charitable infirmary. Two of the inmates were released on the night using the concert's proceeds.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1742 — George Frideric Handel at the Great Music Hall on Fishamble Street, Dublin. The "Hallelujah Chorus" became a standing-ovation custom. It's rumored King George II stood at its London premiere; no contemporary source confirms the story.

events.title: Rhapsody in Blue Premieres
events.blurb: A 25-year-old former Tin Pan Alley song-plugger's first major concert work — a one-movement concerto for piano and jazz band — premiered at a Manhattan concert hall advertised as "An Experiment in Modern Music." The piece's opening clarinet glissando, improvised in rehearsal as a joke, was left in. The concert had begun with banal novelty pieces; by the time the composer walked out to sit at the piano, the audience was dozing. He woke them up.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 1924 — George Gershwin at Aeolian Hall, Manhattan. The bandleader was Paul Whiteman. The audience included Rachmaninoff, Stravinsky, Fritz Kreisler, and Sergei Rachmaninoff. United Airlines has used it as its ad music since 1987.

events.title: Louis Armstrong's Hot Fives
events.blurb: A 24-year-old cornetist who had grown up in the poorest section of New Orleans walked into a Chicago studio for the first session with a small band of his own. Over the next three years, the "Hot Five" and "Hot Seven" sessions would reshape popular music. His vocal improvisation on "Heebie Jeebies" — a chorus of nonsense syllables when he claimed to drop his lyric sheet — launched scat singing. His trumpet solos made the individual improvisation the heart of jazz.
events.revealBlurb: November 12, 1925 — Louis Armstrong at OKeh Records, Chicago. The "Heebie Jeebies" vocal made him a national figure. He would become the first African-American to host a nationally sponsored radio show.

events.title: Strange Fruit Recorded
events.blurb: A 23-year-old African-American singer, in a Manhattan studio, recorded a song about the lynching of Black Americans that had been written by a Jewish high-school teacher from the Bronx. Her regular label refused to release it; a tiny specialty label agreed. She closed with it at every set at her Greenwich Village club, the room going dark except for a spotlight on her face, no encore permitted. The song haunted her for the rest of her short life.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 1939 — Billie Holiday, Commodore Records. Songwriter: Abel Meeropol, under the pen name Lewis Allan. Meeropol and his wife later adopted the two young sons of the executed Ethel and Julius Rosenberg.

events.title: Woodstock Festival Opens
events.blurb: A music festival on a dairy farm in upstate New York that had sold 186,000 advance tickets was overwhelmed by more than 400,000 attendees in the preceding 48 hours, forcing organisers to declare it a free event and abandon the ticket booths. Thirty-two acts performed over four rain-soaked days, and the festival became the defining cultural gathering of its generation.

events.title: The Rigveda Is Composed
events.blurb: Across the Punjab river plains, priestly families called the rishis composed hymns to deities of fire, storm, soma, and dawn, passing them orally from teacher to student with astonishing precision — no written word, just breath and memory. The result was a corpus of 1,028 hymns in 10,552 verses that survives almost perfectly today: the oldest substantial text in any Indo-European language, and the basis of all subsequent Sanskrit literature.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1200 BCE — composed in the Sapta Sindhu (seven rivers) region. Transmitted entirely by memory for at least a millennium before being written down. The oral tradition was so exacting that modern linguistics uses it to reconstruct the pronunciation of proto-Indo-European, a language no one has ever heard.

events.title: Harsha's Assembly Crowns Him Emperor
events.blurb: A 16-year-old prince of Thanesar, whose father and elder brother had recently died, was persuaded by nobles and the king of Kamarupa to assume leadership of a fractured north India. Within six years he had consolidated the largest empire north of the Vindhyas since the Mauryas — and would go on to host the Chinese traveller Xuanzang, compose Sanskrit plays, distribute his treasury to charity every five years, and correspond with Tang-dynasty China.
events.revealBlurb: April 606 CE — Harsha Vardhana, Kannauj. Xuanzang spent years at his court and wrote that Harsha gave away so much treasure at the Prayag festival every five years that by the end he had only his horse and elephant left.

events.title: Rajendra Chola's Navy Crosses the Bay of Bengal
events.blurb: The Chola emperor dispatched a fleet from the Coromandel Coast that crossed the Bay of Bengal, sacked the capital of the Srivijaya empire in Sumatra, captured its king, seized cities along the Malay Peninsula, and imposed Chola trading dominance over the sea lanes between India and China. It was the largest seaborne military operation ever launched from the Indian subcontinent, covering over 3,000 kilometres of open ocean.
events.revealBlurb: 1025 CE — Rajendra Chola I, Tamil Nadu. For the next century, Tamil merchant guilds — the Manigramam and Ainnurruvar — dominated trade from the Malabar coast to present-day Singapore. This is the moment when South India owned the Indian Ocean.

events.title: Guru Nanak Is Born
events.blurb: A child was born to a Khatri family in a Punjab village that is now in Pakistan. At age 30, he reportedly vanished into a river for three days; when he emerged, he proclaimed "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim" and began wandering across Asia — from Sri Lanka to Tibet to Baghdad — singing hymns about the oneness of the formless divine, the equality of all people, and the corruption of caste and ritual. He walked an estimated 28,000 kilometres in his lifetime.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1469 — Guru Nanak Dev Ji, born at Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib, Pakistan). His birthday is celebrated as Gurpurab on the full moon of Kartik. Nanak composed 974 hymns, which form the core of the Guru Granth Sahib — the living, eternal Guru of the Sikh faith.

events.title: Babur Wins the First Battle of Panipat
events.blurb: A Timurid prince from Fergana, having failed to hold Samarkand three times, led a force of 12,000 men and 15 cannons against the Delhi Sultanate's 70,000-strong army and 1,000 war elephants on a flat plain north of Delhi. Using a Central Asian tactic called the tulughma — flanking arcs of cavalry combined with cannon fire — he routed and killed the last Lodi sultan in a single afternoon, ending one dynasty and beginning another.
events.revealBlurb: April 21, 1526 — Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire. His cannons were among the first used on an Indian battlefield. The elephants, terrified by the sound, turned and trampled their own side. Babur wrote about it all in his memoirs, the Baburnama, with the eye of a poet.

events.title: Jackie Robinson Breaks Color Barrier
events.blurb: A 28-year-old second baseman took the field at a Brooklyn ballpark and became the first African-American to play in modern Major League Baseball, breaking a 63-year color line enforced by gentlemen's agreement rather than written rule. He went hitless in his debut but reached base on an error and scored the winning run.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1947 — Ebbets Field, Brooklyn Dodgers. Team president Branch Rickey had signed him with the understanding he would absorb abuse without retaliation for two years. Robinson's number 42 was retired across every MLB team in 1997, the only such universal retirement in sports.

events.title: SNCC Founded
events.blurb: At a North Carolina conference convened by a veteran activist, 200 student sit-in leaders from across the South formed a new grassroots organization to coordinate direct-action campaigns independently of older civil rights groups. The students were younger, more confrontational, and willing to risk their lives; many became the foot soldiers of the Freedom Rides, Freedom Summer, and Selma.
events.revealBlurb: April 17, 1960 — Raleigh, NC. Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, commonly pronounced "snick." Organizer Ella Baker convinced the students to stay independent rather than fold into Martin Luther King's Southern Christian Leadership Conference. Stokely Carmichael led it during the "Black Power" turn in 1966.

events.title: Freedom Riders Depart
events.blurb: Thirteen volunteers — seven Black, six white — boarded buses in Washington, D.C. bound for New Orleans to test a recent Supreme Court ruling outlawing segregated interstate travel facilities. In Alabama their bus was firebombed outside Anniston and the riders beaten bloody by a mob in Birmingham. They kept riding. Subsequent waves continued through the summer.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1961 — sponsored by CORE. A 21-year-old John Lewis was among them and had his skull fractured. Attorney General Robert Kennedy called for a "cooling-off period;" CORE leader James Farmer replied: "We've been cooling off for 100 years."

events.title: Stonewall Riots
events.blurb: A routine police raid on a Mafia-owned gay bar in a Greenwich Village of Manhattan turned into a six-night uprising when patrons — many of them drag queens, street kids, and trans people of color — fought back rather than submit to arrest. The confrontation catalyzed the modern LGBTQ rights movement; the first Pride marches were held on its first anniversary.
events.revealBlurb: June 28, 1969 — Stonewall Inn, NYC. Pivotal figures included Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera. The riot ignited the Gay Liberation Front, which modeled itself on the Black Panthers. June is now Pride Month across much of the world.

events.title: MLK Day Signed
events.blurb: After 15 years of advocacy by civil rights leaders, Congress passed and the president signed legislation establishing the third Monday of January as a federal holiday honoring the slain civil rights leader. The fight to pass it had drawn bitter opposition from some senators, including one who conducted a 16-day filibuster. It became the first federal holiday commemorating an African-American.
events.revealBlurb: November 2, 1983 — Ronald Reagan. Arizona voters rejected recognizing the holiday in 1990; the NFL moved the 1993 Super Bowl from Phoenix in response, and the state reversed course. New Hampshire, the last holdout, adopted it in 1999.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Cabral Reaches Brazil
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Portuguese nobleman commanding a 13-ship expedition bound for India — following Vasco da Gama's recent route — sailed so far west to catch favourable trade winds that he accidentally made landfall on a South American coast later named after a dyewood tree. He claimed it for Portugal under the six-year-old Tordesillas line and continued on to India. The accidental detour is the conventional starting point of Brazilian history.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1500 — Pedro Álvares Cabral in modern Bahia. He called the land "Ilha de Vera Cruz." Some historians think the "accidental" landfall was deliberate, responding to intelligence Portuguese mariners had gathered earlier. He lost six ships and over 100 men to storms en route onward to India.

events.title: Luther at the Diet of Worms
events.blurb: A 37-year-old German theologian, summoned to a Rhineland imperial assembly under a guarantee of safe conduct, was asked to recant his written attacks on papal authority. He asked for a day to consider; the next day he returned and refused unless shown his error from scripture. The emperor placed him under imperial ban the following month. He would have been executed if the elector of Saxony had not hidden him in a castle, where he translated the New Testament into German.
events.revealBlurb: April 17-18, 1521 — Martin Luther before Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. The famous line "Here I stand; I can do no other" may be apocryphal; it appeared only in a printed account issued after the events. Luther lived another 25 years, marrying, fathering six children, and publishing prolifically.

events.title: Jamestown Colony Founded
events.blurb: English settlers dispatched by the Virginia Company came ashore on a low, marshy peninsula in the tidewater and drove stakes for the first permanent English settlement in the territory that would become the United States. Of the roughly 104 men and boys who arrived, fewer than 40 survived their first year, undone by brackish drinking water, starvation, and disease.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1607 — Virginia. The site was chosen partly because its deep water let ships dock without anchors — and partly because it looked easy to defend. It was also mosquito-ridden and had no fresh water. Within nine months, roughly 65% of the colonists were dead.

events.title: Charles I Beheaded
events.blurb: An English king, convicted of high treason by a specially-convened parliamentary court after losing two civil wars against his own Parliament, was beheaded outside a London banqueting house on a platform erected for the purpose, watched by a large silent crowd. He wore two shirts to keep from shivering in the cold, lest witnesses think him afraid. It was the first judicial execution of a reigning European monarch. Eleven years of republican Commonwealth followed before his son was restored to the throne.
events.revealBlurb: January 30, 1649 — Charles I outside Whitehall Palace. The executioner wore a mask and wig; his identity has never been confirmed. Oliver Cromwell would dominate the subsequent Commonwealth; his corpse was dug up and symbolically "executed" in 1661 after the restoration.

events.title: Army-McCarthy Hearings
events.blurb: A televised congressional inquiry pit a grandstanding senator against the U.S. Army, which he had accused of harboring subversives. Over 36 days, 20 million Americans watched live as his bullying tactics eroded public sympathy. The defining moment came when a quiet Boston lawyer turned to him and asked, "Have you no sense of decency, sir?"
events.revealBlurb: April 22 to June 17, 1954 — the lawyer was Joseph Welch. His line came on June 9, after McCarthy attacked a young associate. Six months later the Senate voted 67-22 to censure McCarthy. He drank himself to death within three years.

events.title: Bay of Pigs Invasion
events.blurb: A brigade of 1,400 Cuban exiles, trained and armed by the CIA, landed on a remote beach on their home island hoping to spark a popular uprising against its revolutionary government. Promised U.S. air support was withheld at the last moment. Within three days all the invaders were dead or captured. A young American president took public responsibility for the fiasco.
events.revealBlurb: April 17-20, 1961 — Kennedy, in office just three months, had inherited the plan from Eisenhower. His approval rating actually rose afterward; he quipped, "the worse I do, the more popular I get." The captured exiles were ransomed for $53 million in food and medicine.

events.title: SDI Announced
events.blurb: In a televised address from the Oval Office, a U.S. president proposed a space-based missile defense shield intended to render nuclear weapons "impotent and obsolete." Critics dubbed it "Star Wars" and scientists called it technically unachievable. Whatever its technical merits, the announcement terrified the Kremlin and forced Soviet planners to contemplate a ruinous new arms race they could not afford.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 1983 — Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative. It never produced a working system, but it contributed to Soviet economic exhaustion. Some historians credit SDI with accelerating Gorbachev's arms-control pivot by years.

events.title: Chernobyl Disaster
events.blurb: During a safety test at the No. 4 reactor of a Ukrainian nuclear power plant, a power surge, flawed reactor design, and operator errors combined to blow the 1,000-tonne reactor lid off the building and send a radioactive plume across Europe. Swedish sensors detected the contamination before Moscow admitted anything had happened. The exclusion zone around the plant remains largely uninhabited nearly forty years on.
events.revealBlurb: April 26, 1986 — 1:23 AM. Two workers died in the initial explosion; 28 firefighters and operators died of acute radiation poisoning in the months after. Roughly 350,000 people were permanently evacuated. Cleanup cost the USSR an estimated 18 billion rubles.

events.title: INF Treaty Signed
events.blurb: At a White House ceremony, the American and Soviet leaders signed a treaty requiring both sides to destroy every intermediate-range nuclear missile they possessed — the first arms-control agreement that actually cut existing weapons rather than capping their growth. Within three years, 2,692 missiles had been verifiably dismantled.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1987 — Reagan and Gorbachev. Both Pershing IIs and SS-20s were eliminated. The treaty was abandoned in 2019 after mutual accusations of cheating, ending a 32-year cornerstone of European security.

events.title: Atlantic Charter
events.blurb: The leader of a neutral superpower and the leader of a beleaguered island nation met secretly aboard warships anchored off a foggy Newfoundland coast and jointly published a declaration of eight principles for the postwar world — including self-determination for peoples, freedom of the seas, and disarmament of aggressor nations — without committing either country to fight.
events.revealBlurb: August 14, 1941 — FDR and Churchill issued the Atlantic Charter from HMS Prince of Wales and USS Augusta in Placentia Bay. The US was still technically neutral. The document became the founding framework for the United Nations. Churchill later noted that when the two men sang "O God Our Help in Ages Past" on deck, he felt the war was won.

events.title: Doolittle Raid on Tokyo
events.blurb: Sixteen medium bombers took off from the pitching deck of an aircraft carrier 650 miles out at sea — far beyond the designed launch range — and struck the enemy's capital and four other cities in daylight, causing minimal physical damage but shattering the belief that the home islands were invulnerable to aerial attack.
events.revealBlurb: April 18, 1942 — Lieutenant Colonel Jimmy Doolittle led 16 B-25 Mitchells off USS Hornet. None of the aircraft had enough fuel to land at friendly bases; crews ditched in China or the Soviet Union. Of 80 raiders, 3 were killed in the attacks and 8 were captured by Japan — 3 of those were executed.

events.title: Warsaw Ghetto Uprising
events.blurb: On the eve of a major Jewish holiday, lightly armed fighters inside an urban ghetto launched a sustained armed resistance against a force sent to complete its deportation to killing centres — holding out for nearly a month against SS troops, armoured vehicles, and systematic building-by-building destruction before the last pockets were overcome.
events.revealBlurb: April 19 – May 16, 1943. The ZOB fighters had roughly 220 pistols, several dozen rifles, and a small supply of grenades and Molotov cocktails. SS commander Jürgen Stroop demolished the Great Synagogue of Warsaw as a symbolic finale on May 16, declaring: "The Jewish quarter of Warsaw is no more." He was hanged in Warsaw in 1952.

events.title: Warsaw Uprising
events.blurb: A resistance army launched an all-out urban insurrection timed to coincide with an approaching allied army's arrival at the city's eastern bank, intending to liberate the capital before that army entered — but the expected support never came, leaving 40,000 fighters and 200,000 civilians to a 63-day battle against overwhelming force that ended in total destruction.
events.revealBlurb: August 1 – October 2, 1944. The Polish Home Army rose at 5:00 PM on August 1 with roughly 40,000 fighters. The approaching Soviet Army halted on the opposite bank and waited. Stalin also denied Allied planes permission to use Soviet airfields for supply drops for weeks. An estimated 200,000 civilians were killed; survivors were expelled and the city was systematically demolished.

events.title: Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima
events.blurb: A single aircraft flying at high altitude released a single bomb over a mid-sized city at 8:15 in the morning, detonating it 600 metres above a distinctive T-shaped bridge with the force of 15,000 tons of TNT — flattening 13 square kilometres, killing between 70,000 and 80,000 people instantly, and ultimately causing 140,000 deaths by the end of the year.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — B-29 Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets, dropped "Little Boy" over Hiroshima. The aiming point was the Aioi Bridge. The bomb missed by about 250 metres but it did not matter. Tibbets's mother's name was Enola Gay. The co-pilot, Robert Lewis, wrote in his journal: "My God, what have we done?"

events.title: Battles of Lexington and Concord
events.blurb: That spring morning, British regulars marching to seize a colonial weapons cache at Concord, Massachusetts, exchanged fire with local militia at Lexington before the colonists scattered; at Concord's North Bridge, a second volley triggered a running battle that chased the redcoats back to Boston. The day produced roughly 300 total casualties and the phrase "the shot heard round the world."
events.revealBlurb: April 19, 1775 — Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts. Nobody knows who fired first at Lexington — colonial accounts and British accounts flatly contradict each other. The phrase "shot heard round the world" was written by Ralph Waldo Emerson in 1837, over 60 years after the fact.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Ratified
events.blurb: New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify the proposed Constitution, providing the three-fourths supermajority required to bring the new framework of government into effect and replace the faltering Articles of Confederation. The document created a federal republic with three separated branches of power — a design that had no exact precedent in world history.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1788 — New Hampshire. Rhode Island didn't ratify until May 1790 — over a year after the government had already begun operating. North Carolina waited until November 1789, after the First Congress had already convened.

events.title: Marbury v. Madison: Judicial Review Established
events.blurb: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the unanimous Supreme Court opinion in a case about a disputed judicial appointment, using it to announce that federal courts possessed the power to strike down laws they found incompatible with the Constitution — a power the Constitution itself does not explicitly mention. The ruling transformed the Supreme Court from the weakest branch of government into an equal arbiter of constitutional meaning.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1803 — Washington, D.C. Marshall's genius was ruling against Marbury (who wanted his commission) so Jefferson couldn't refuse to comply, while simultaneously claiming the Court's enormous new power. Jefferson privately hated the decision but was trapped. The ruling wasn't used to strike down another law for 54 more years.

events.title: Pullman Strike and Federal Injunction
events.blurb: When the Pullman Company cut wages by 25 percent without reducing rents in its company-owned town south of Chicago, nearly 4,000 workers walked out that spring; within weeks, the American Railway Union's boycott of Pullman cars had paralyzed rail traffic across 29 railroads and 27 states. President Grover Cleveland dispatched federal troops and obtained a court injunction to break the strike, establishing the federal government's willingness to use military force against organized labor.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1894 — Pullman, Illinois. Eugene Debs, the ARU leader, served six months in federal prison for defying the injunction — and read socialist literature in his cell, emerging as America's most famous socialist. The strike also created Labor Day as a federal holiday, rushed through Congress as a conciliation gesture two days before Debs was arrested.

events.title: Spanish-American War Declaration
events.blurb: The United States declared war on Spain following the mysterious explosion of the battleship USS Maine in Havana Harbor and years of lurid coverage of Spanish atrocities in Cuba by the American yellow press. The 114-day conflict ended Spanish colonial rule in Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines, and announced the United States as a Pacific and Caribbean imperial power.
events.revealBlurb: April 25, 1898 — Washington, D.C. Theodore Roosevelt resigned as Assistant Secretary of the Navy to lead the volunteer Rough Riders cavalry regiment, charging up San Juan Hill — a battle that took one afternoon and made him president. Secretary of State John Hay called it "a splendid little war."

events.title: Shaanxi Earthquake
events.blurb: The deadliest earthquake in recorded human history struck a densely populated region of northern China in the early morning, collapsing hillsides dotted with cave dwellings carved from soft loess soil. Roughly 830,000 people died — some 60 percent of the population of the affected counties. In some districts, everyone was killed.
events.revealBlurb: January 23, 1556 — Shaanxi Province, Ming Dynasty. The loess hillsides, prized for their insulation, became mass graves when the quake liquefied them. The toll remains a single-event record four and a half centuries later.

events.title: Kobe Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 6.9 earthquake struck a major Japanese port city in the early morning, collapsing expressway sections and igniting fires that destroyed some 7,000 wooden houses. 6,434 people died. The initial government response was famously sluggish — organized yakuza crime syndicates distributed relief supplies before the army arrived.
events.revealBlurb: January 17, 1995 — Kobe. The elevated Hanshin Expressway fell sideways onto its support pillars, a widely published image of post-war Japanese infrastructure failure. The Aum Shinrikyo cult's Tokyo subway sarin attack followed two months later, making 1995 a traumatic year for Japan.

events.title: Eyjafjallajökull Eruption
events.blurb: A glacier-capped volcano in Iceland erupted, sending a plume of fine silicate ash into the jet stream. Authorities across Europe, uncertain about engine safety, grounded all commercial aviation for six days. Around 10 million passengers were stranded, and global airlines lost an estimated $1.7 billion. Few people died, but the event showed how fragile modern mobility had become.
events.revealBlurb: April 14-20, 2010 — Iceland. The volcano's name became a running joke for newscasters. Stranded travelers included heads of state on their way to a funeral in Poland; many drove for days to get home. Rental car companies had their biggest week ever.

events.title: Deepwater Horizon Spill
events.blurb: A blowout on a semi-submersible drilling rig in the Gulf of Mexico killed 11 workers and severed the riser pipe to a well 1,500 metres below the surface. Over the next 87 days, as engineers tried increasingly improbable methods to cap it, roughly 780 million litres of crude oil gushed into the sea — the largest accidental marine oil spill in history.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 2010 — off Louisiana. The well was finally killed in mid-September. BP paid over $65 billion in settlements, fines, and cleanup. A live-stream of the ocean-floor plume was watched by millions during the crisis; executives who claimed it was "relatively tiny" became memes.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Declared
events.blurb: The World Health Organization, having watched a novel coronavirus spread from a single city to 114 countries in ten weeks, formally upgraded its assessment from epidemic to pandemic. Within days, much of the world entered some form of lockdown — schools shut, flights grounded, stock markets crashed. Before vaccines arrived a year later, it would kill millions.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2020 — WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. The first known case had been reported in Wuhan in early December 2019. Official global death toll exceeded 7 million; excess mortality studies suggest the real number is closer to 20 million.

events.title: September 11 Attacks
events.blurb: Nineteen hijackers affiliated with al-Qaeda commandeered four commercial airliners on a Tuesday morning, crashing two into the twin towers of a Manhattan financial complex, one into a Pentagon wing, and one into a Pennsylvania field after passengers fought back. Both World Trade Center towers collapsed within two hours. 2,977 people died. The attacks reshaped American foreign policy, launched two wars that lasted the next two decades, and redefined commercial aviation security for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 2001 — orchestrated by Osama bin Laden. United States entered Afghanistan in October 2001 and Iraq in March 2003. The 9/11 Memorial & Museum opened on the site in 2014; One World Trade Center, topped out in 2013, is the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere.

events.title: American Idol Premieres
events.blurb: A singing-competition reality show — adapted from a British format — premiered on Fox with a caustic British music executive as its lead judge, flanked by two milder American ones. The first season's audition rounds and final contestant-viewer-vote format drew enormous audiences; its first winner, a 20-year-old Texan waitress, became a genuine pop star. The show's stern British judge became a cultural shorthand for merciless critique.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 2002 — judges Simon Cowell, Paula Abdul, Randy Jackson. Host Ryan Seacrest. Season 1 winner Kelly Clarkson went on to a successful music and TV career. American Idol ran on Fox until 2016 and was revived on ABC in 2018; Clarkson's "A Moment Like This" is still its most famous product.

events.title: Whitney Houston Dies
events.blurb: A 48-year-old American singer with one of the most powerful voices in pop music history was found unresponsive in a bathtub at a Beverly Hills hotel. The cause of death was accidental drowning complicated by heart disease and cocaine use. She had been scheduled to attend a Grammy Awards pre-party that evening. Her death came the night before the Grammys themselves, which had to be hastily rewritten to include a tribute. Seven years later her only daughter would die under similar circumstances.
events.revealBlurb: February 11, 2012 — Whitney Houston at the Beverly Hilton. Daughter Bobbi Kristina Brown, 22, was found unresponsive in a bathtub on January 31, 2015 and died six months later. Houston's "I Will Always Love You" had been the bestselling single by a woman in history until Adele surpassed it.

events.title: Prince Dies
events.blurb: A 57-year-old American musician was found unresponsive in an elevator at his Paisley Park estate and recording studio outside Minneapolis, having died alone of an accidental fentanyl overdose. He had been taking painkillers for chronic hip pain aggravated by decades of acrobatic stage performances. His catalogue — 39 studio albums, countless B-sides and unreleased tracks — was so extensive that new material continued to surface from his vault for years after his death.
events.revealBlurb: April 21, 2016 — Prince Rogers Nelson. He had no valid will; the distribution of his $156 million estate involved his six siblings and took six years of litigation to resolve. The tribute concerts in the weeks after his death included a Saturday Night Live special and coverage on every major music broadcast.

events.title: Notre-Dame Fire
events.blurb: A fire that began in the attic of an 850-year-old Gothic cathedral on an island in the Seine at the heart of Paris burned for nine hours, collapsing the 93-metre 19th-century spire and destroying two-thirds of the roof. Firefighters managed to save the main stone structure, the two bell towers, the three great rose windows, and most of the interior artworks. Notre-Dame's silhouette without its spire, broadcast live to the world, became a modern visual shock.
events.revealBlurb: April 15-16, 2019 — cause never conclusively determined; probably an electrical fault or a discarded cigarette. French President Emmanuel Macron pledged to reopen the cathedral within five years; it reopened December 7, 2024, more or less on schedule.

events.title: Mosaic Browser Released
events.blurb: Undergraduate students at a University of Illinois supercomputing centre released a graphical web browser for Unix, with a version for Windows and Mac released later in the year. Unlike the earlier terminal-based browsers, it could display images inline with text. Within 18 months, web traffic had grown by 10,000 percent. The browser's lead developer would leave to co-found a company that would dominate the next phase.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1993 — developed at the NCSA, lead developer Marc Andreessen. Andreessen co-founded Netscape within a year. Mosaic was free for non-commercial use, a decision that gave the web the critical mass it needed.
