events.title: iTunes Store Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched an online music store selling individual songs for 99 cents each, a pricing decision its CEO had to personally negotiate with record-label executives deeply suspicious of any further internet disruption. The store sold a million downloads in its first six days. Within four years, it was the largest music retailer in the United States.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 2003 — Apple. Steve Jobs had threaten to "pull the plug" on the negotiations at one point. The catalogue launched with 200,000 songs, Mac-only; Windows compatibility came in October. The per-song price model reshaped the music industry.

events.title: Facebook Launched
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore with a history of making unauthorized student-directory sites launched, from his dorm room, a social network restricted to students with harvard.edu email addresses. It reached half the Harvard student body within two weeks. He expanded to Yale, Columbia, and Stanford within weeks. Within a year he had dropped out; within four he was a billionaire on paper.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2004 — Mark Zuckerberg at Harvard, with co-founders Eduardo Saverin, Andrew McCollum, Dustin Moskovitz, and Chris Hughes. Originally thefacebook.com. Zuckerberg settled with the Winklevoss twins for $65 million in 2008; they spent it on Bitcoin.

events.title: Instagram Launched
events.blurb: A two-person startup released a free iOS app that let users take photos, apply one of eleven retro filters, and share them to a simple timeline-based social network. It acquired 25,000 users on launch day and its first million within three months. Facebook bought the company for $1 billion in cash and stock eighteen months later, when it had thirteen employees and zero revenue.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 2010 — Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger. Originally built as a location-based check-in app called Burbn. The $1 billion Facebook acquisition in April 2012 is now considered one of the great bargains in tech history.

events.title: Snapchat Launched
events.blurb: Three Stanford undergraduates released an iOS app that let users send photos that automatically disappeared a few seconds after being viewed. One founder had pitched the idea for a product-design class the previous spring and been told it was terrible. The app would grow explosively as a teenage-first social platform and introduce "Stories," a format quickly copied by every major competitor.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 2011 — Evan Spiegel, Bobby Murphy, and Reggie Brown. Originally named Picaboo. Facebook offered to acquire Snap for $3 billion in 2013; Spiegel said no. Snap went public in 2017 at a $24 billion valuation.

events.title: Monteverdi's Orfeo Premieres
events.blurb: A 39-year-old Italian composer staged a setting of the Orpheus myth at a ducal palace in a northern Italian city, combining recitative, arias, choruses, and instrumental ritornellos in a way earlier experimental works had only gestured at. The resulting five-act piece is considered the first opera that remains in the regular performance repertoire. Only two printed scores of the work survive.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1607 — Claudio Monteverdi at the court of the Gonzagas in Mantua. The orchestra called for some 40 instruments. The character of Orpheus was sung by tenor Francesco Rasi; the audience was tiny — members of the Accademia degli Invaghiti.

events.title: Bach Dedicates Brandenburg Concertos
events.blurb: A 36-year-old German court composer, looking for a new job, sent a margrave a set of six concerto grossi he had been accumulating over several years. The dedication was effusive; he apologized for the "vast distance between his person and the margrave." The margrave never acknowledged the gift, let alone hired him, and probably never had them performed. The manuscripts sat in a Prussian archive for 128 years before rediscovery.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1721 — Johann Sebastian Bach, addressing Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg. The scores were narrowly rescued from Allied bombing in 1945. The music now exists thanks to a librarian who grabbed them as he fled Leipzig for the Harz mountains.

events.title: Dylan Goes Electric
events.blurb: A 24-year-old folk singer, backed by a ragged rhythm section from the previous night's acquaintance, walked onto the stage of a folk festival on a Rhode Island pier with a sunburst Stratocaster slung low over his shoulder. He played three short electric songs before some boos drowned out the applause. He walked off, returned with his acoustic, and played two more. The event marked, depending on who tells it, the birth of folk-rock or the betrayal of American folk.
events.revealBlurb: July 25, 1965 — Bob Dylan at the Newport Folk Festival. Pete Seeger, legend says, tried to cut the sound cables with an axe. Seeger later denied it. The songs included "Maggie's Farm" and "Like a Rolling Stone." Dylan's next tour was booed nightly for a year.

events.title: John Lennon Shot
events.blurb: A 40-year-old former Beatle, returning to his Manhattan apartment building with his wife after a late-night recording session, was shot four times in the back at close range by a young man he had signed an autograph for earlier that afternoon. He was pronounced dead at a nearby hospital 20 minutes later. Vigils were held around the world. His wife asked that his birthday be celebrated with international moments of silence, which has since become a yearly tradition.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1980 — John Lennon at The Dakota, NYC. Shooter Mark David Chapman remains in prison, denied parole 13 times. Lennon's album "Double Fantasy" had been released three weeks earlier; it took on enormous posthumous sales.

events.title: Beyoncé's Lemonade Released
events.blurb: A 34-year-old singer dropped a surprise sixth studio album, released simultaneously with a 65-minute accompanying visual film that aired on a premium cable channel. The album and film explored, over 12 tracks, themes of infidelity, race, and Black Southern heritage. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and became the only album to receive the highest score possible from Metacritic at the time. The cultural moment was so saturating that a vegetable-based cocktail name briefly came into common use.
events.revealBlurb: April 23, 2016 — Beyoncé. Film featured collaborators including Warsan Shire (poetry) and Kahlil Joseph (co-direction). The Tidal-exclusive release infuriated fans of other streaming services and drew attention to Jay-Z's struggling platform.

events.title: Viking 1 First Mars Landing
events.blurb: NASA's Viking 1 lander touched down on Chryse Planitia, becoming the first spacecraft to successfully land on Mars and operate on its surface. Within minutes it returned the first color photographs of the Martian surface and began a biology experiment suite designed to detect signs of microbial life — whose results remain contested among planetary scientists.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1976 — Viking 1. The landing date was chosen deliberately: it was the seventh anniversary of the Apollo 11 Moon landing. Viking 1 operated for 2,245 Martian days — more than six Earth years — before its final transmission. One biology experiment produced an initially positive result for life that NASA later attributed to reactive soil chemistry.

events.title: Voyager 1 Launch
events.blurb: NASA launched Voyager 1 on a trajectory exploiting a once-in-176-year alignment of the outer planets, allowing a single spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn using gravitational slingshots. The probe carries a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing sounds, music, and images representing life on Earth, selected by a committee chaired by Carl Sagan.
events.revealBlurb: September 5, 1977 — Voyager 1. It launched 16 days after its twin, Voyager 2, yet arrived at Jupiter first due to a faster trajectory. In 2012 it became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. As of 2024 it is more than 24 billion km from Earth — so far that its radio signals, traveling at light speed, take over 22 hours to arrive.

events.title: Hubble Space Telescope Launch
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Discovery deployed the Hubble Space Telescope into a 612 km orbit, positioning a 2.4-meter primary mirror above Earth's atmosphere to capture ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light without atmospheric distortion. The primary mirror was later found to have been ground 2.2 micrometers too flat — a spherical aberration correctable only by a servicing mission.
events.revealBlurb: April 24, 1990 — STS-31. The mirror flaw came from a testing lens installed backward by 1.3 mm. Three years later, astronauts installed corrective optics during the first Hubble servicing mission — essentially fitting the telescope with contact lenses. Hubble has since produced more than 1.5 million observations.

events.title: ISS First Crewed Occupation
events.blurb: A three-person crew docked a Soyuz capsule to the International Space Station's Zvezda module at 09:21 UTC, beginning a continuous human presence in low Earth orbit that has not been interrupted since. The station at that point consisted of three connected modules spanning roughly 27 meters, a fraction of its eventual 109-meter length.
events.revealBlurb: November 2, 2000 — Expedition 1. Commander Bill Shepherd radioed NASA to request the station's call sign be changed from "Alpha" to "International Space Station" — a small act of diplomacy that stuck. The crew of two Russians and one American had access to less than 425 cubic meters of living space, about the volume of a large school bus.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: Electron Announced
events.blurb: During a lecture at a London scientific institution, a physicist announced that cathode rays were composed of particles roughly one-thousandth the mass of a hydrogen atom — the first demonstration that atoms were not the smallest units of matter. The particles were initially called "corpuscles"; the modern name came from a suggestion by an Irish physicist the same year.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1897 — J.J. Thomson's discovery won him the Nobel Prize in 1906, and his son George Thomson won a separate Nobel in 1937 for proving the electron was a wave. Father and son together proved it was a particle and a wave — one of physics' neatest family rivalries.

events.title: Radium Announced
events.blurb: A husband-and-wife chemistry team announced the isolation of a new radioactive element extracted from several tonnes of pitchblende ore, reporting it was approximately 900 times more radioactive than uranium. The woman researcher would go on to become the first person to win two Nobel Prizes in different scientific disciplines.

events.title: Pluto Discovered
events.blurb: A young farm-hand-turned-astronomer at an Arizona observatory found a faint, slowly moving point of light by comparing photographic plates taken several days apart — a new body at the edge of the solar system. The discovery completed a decadelong search for a hypothetical ninth planet believed to be perturbing the orbits of the outermost known worlds.
events.revealBlurb: February 18, 1930 — Clyde Tombaugh was 24 and had never attended university. The name "Pluto" was suggested by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl in Oxford, via her grandfather. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a "dwarf planet," prompting widespread public outrage and several state legislatures to pass resolutions disagreeing.

events.title: DNA Double Helix Published
events.blurb: A two-page letter in the journal Nature described a double-helical structure for deoxyribonucleic acid, with two chains running in opposite directions held together by hydrogen bonds between paired bases. The authors noted their structure immediately suggested a mechanism by which genetic information could be copied.
events.revealBlurb: April 25, 1953 — Watson and Crick, aided by Rosalind Franklin's unpublished X-ray diffraction image known as "Photo 51". Their famous closing line: "It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism" — one of science's great understatements.

events.title: Endosymbiotic Theory Published
events.blurb: A paper proposed that the energy-producing mitochondria and photosynthetic chloroplasts inside complex cells were originally free-living bacteria that had been engulfed by a host cell and retained over billions of years — a radical claim that the cell's most vital structures were once independent organisms. The paper had been rejected by approximately fifteen journals before finding a publisher.
events.revealBlurb: June 1967 — Lynn Margulis submitted the paper under her married surname Sagan; it became one of biology's most-cited papers after decades of derision. Her critics called it "too fantastic." When the hypothesis was tested by comparing DNA in mitochondria to bacterial DNA in the 1980s, it matched almost exactly.

events.title: Oprah's "You Get a Car!"
events.blurb: An American daytime talk-show host opened her show's 19th-season premiere by giving a brand-new compact sedan to each of 276 audience members who, she said, had been nominated by loved ones as desperately needing a new vehicle. She turned to a different audience section and shouted: "You get a car! You get a car!" each audience member in turn. The sustained joy — and the full-volume shouting — became a lasting cultural moment captured in countless memes and parodies.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 2004 — Oprah Winfrey on The Oprah Winfrey Show. The cars were Pontiac G6 sedans donated by General Motors, which covered the ~$7 million cost as a promotion. Audience members were reportedly shocked to discover the IRS expected them to pay tax on the "gift" of around $7,000.

events.title: Heath Ledger Dies
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Australian actor was found dead in his lower Manhattan apartment by a masseuse who had come for an appointment. The cause was an accidental overdose of six prescription medications, including painkillers, anti-anxiety drugs, and sleep aids. He had recently finished filming an intense performance as the Joker in a Batman film released six months later; his family and colleagues have long disputed the "Joker-drove-him-mad" narrative that emerged. He won a posthumous Academy Award for the role.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 2008 — Heath Ledger in NYC. Daughter Matilda (with Michelle Williams) was 2. His 2008 film "The Dark Knight" was one of the first films to benefit from the surge in digital IMAX releases. His posthumous Oscar made him the second actor ever to win a competitive acting Oscar after death.

events.title: Balloon Boy Hoax
events.blurb: A Colorado family reported that their 6-year-old son had been carried aloft in a homemade silver mylar weather balloon that had drifted off from their backyard. National news networks covered the balloon's two-hour, 80-kilometre flight live, interrupting regular programming. The balloon landed empty. The boy was found hiding in the family attic. Within a day, the father admitted the whole thing had been a publicity stunt, hoping to land the family a reality-TV show.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2009 — Heene family, Fort Collins, CO. The father Richard Heene was convicted of a felony and served 30 days; the mother Mayumi got misdemeanor charges. The Heenes reportedly received a pardon from Colorado governor Jared Polis in December 2020.

events.title: William and Kate Wedding
events.blurb: The 28-year-old second-in-line heir to the British throne married his 29-year-old university sweetheart at Westminster Abbey in London before a congregation of 1,900 and a global TV audience estimated at 2 billion. The bride wore a long-sleeved ivory lace gown; the couple kissed twice on the Buckingham Palace balcony. The marriage, closely followed by the British tabloids for years, has so far produced three children and remained notably less turbulent than the equivalent royal marriage of the generation before.
events.revealBlurb: April 29, 2011 — Prince William and Catherine Middleton. William succeeded his father Charles as Prince of Wales when Charles became king in September 2022. Their three children, in line to the throne: George (2013), Charlotte (2015), Louis (2018).

events.title: Osama bin Laden Killed
events.blurb: A team of US Navy SEALs, helicoptered into the Pakistani city of Abbottabad at night, stormed a walled compound where the founder of al-Qaeda had been hiding for over five years, 1.3 kilometres from Pakistan's premier military academy. He was killed in the raid, along with four others. His body was buried at sea from a US carrier to prevent his grave becoming a pilgrimage site. The president announced the operation in a late-night television address; crowds gathered outside the White House chanting "USA."
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 2011 — Operation Neptune Spear. SEAL Team Six; President Barack Obama. Bin Laden had orchestrated the September 11, 2001 attacks. His death ended a 9-year, 8-month manhunt. The compound was demolished months later by the Pakistani government.

events.title: Metropolis Released
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Austrian director released a 153-minute silent epic — at the time the most expensive film ever made — set in a stratified future city where wealthy elites enjoy skyscraper gardens above an underground inferno of machine-tending workers. The film's visual language — robot maidens, neon skylines, expressionist sets — shaped science-fiction imagery for the next century. The premiere had uneven reception; 40 minutes of footage were later cut.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 1927 — Fritz Lang at the UFA-Palast am Zoo, Berlin. A reasonably complete version was pieced together only in 2008, when a 16mm print from the 1930s was found in a Buenos Aires archive. The robot Maria was voted the most important film robot in history.

events.title: Citizen Kane Released
events.blurb: A 25-year-old radio and theatre prodigy made his feature film directing debut with a quasi-biographical study of a newspaper tycoon, structurally organized as a series of flashback interviews about the man's last word ("Rosebud"). The film used deep-focus cinematography, low-angle setups, overlapping dialogue, and non-linear structure in ways that rewrote the cinematic grammar of the next 70 years. Its real-life subject, a media baron, tried to have every print destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1941 — Orson Welles, age 25. The target was William Randolph Hearst, who banned mention of the film in his newspapers. It lost Best Picture to "How Green Was My Valley." It tops nearly every "greatest films of all time" list.

events.title: Seven Samurai Released
events.blurb: A Japanese director released a 207-minute epic about a defenseless farming village that hires seven masterless samurai to protect it from annual bandit raids. The film's action-adventure template — a diverse team of skilled specialists assembled for a dangerous mission — has been imitated in countless subsequent movies across every genre. One of its rainy climactic battles required 18 weeks of shooting and 500 tons of supplemental water.
events.revealBlurb: April 26, 1954 — Akira Kurosawa, starring Toshiro Mifune. The film was remade by Hollywood six years later as "The Magnificent Seven." The 2016 Marvel film "The Avengers" has been called, by its own director, a direct descendant.

events.title: Toy Story Released
events.blurb: A California animation studio released the first feature film produced entirely with computer-generated imagery, a 81-minute buddy comedy about a child's cowboy doll who feels threatened by a new space-ranger action figure. The studio had spent four years on the film, through three near-cancellations and total rewrites; the resulting picture grossed $390 million and established a new production studio as the dominant force in animation for the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1995 — Pixar Animation Studios, directed by John Lasseter. Tom Hanks and Tim Allen voiced Woody and Buzz Lightyear. Pixar had been Apple founder Steve Jobs's expensive side-project; Disney bought them for $7.4 billion in 2006.

events.title: Spirited Away Wins Oscar
events.blurb: A Japanese animated film about a 10-year-old girl's adventure in a bathhouse for spirits won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, an unprecedented achievement for an Asian work in the category. The film's director, then 62, had been making animated features for decades, but most American audiences had never heard of him or his studio. The Oscar made the director a household name and put his studio's catalog on every arthouse wishlist.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2003 — Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli's film won Best Animated Feature. Miyazaki did not attend the ceremony in protest of the Iraq War. "Spirited Away" remains Japan's highest-grossing film and grossed over $395 million worldwide.

events.title: Raja Harishchandra Released
events.blurb: A mythological silent film about the legendarily truthful king Harishchandra — shot in Bombay using an all-male cast because no actress would agree to appear on screen — opened at the Coronation Cinematograph in Girgaon and became India's first feature film, running 3,700 feet of hand-cranked footage. Its creator had spent over a year learning to develop film himself after being refused laboratory access.
events.revealBlurb: May 3, 1913 — Dadasaheb Phalke's debut. He was a printer by trade. Legend says he watched The Life of Christ (1906) in Bombay and decided India needed its own screen mythology. All the female roles were played by male wrestlers and cooks; no respectable woman would work in pictures.

events.title: Film and Television Institute of India Founded
events.blurb: A national school for cinema craft, established on the former premises of a shuttered studio whose golden era had passed, began training directors, cinematographers, and sound engineers in a new medium that independent India wanted to shape on its own terms. Its graduates would go on to redefine the aesthetic vocabulary of both art-house and popular Indian filmmaking.
events.revealBlurb: 1960, Pune. Built inside the Prabhat Film Company compound. Satyajit Ray advised on its curriculum. Early graduates include Shyam Benegal, Adoor Gopalakrishnan, Mrinal Sen, Girish Karnad — essentially the entire generation that invented Indian parallel cinema.

events.title: Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai Released
events.blurb: A double-role romantic thriller built around a completely unknown actor — son of its director — became the highest-grossing Hindi film of the year and won 92 awards across ceremonies, a figure the Guinness World Records certified as a record for any single film. The overnight stardom it generated was so total that magazine covers, television specials, and public hysteria followed within days.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 2000 — directed by Rakesh Roshan, launching his son Hrithik. The film began production before Hrithik had done a single screen test beyond his father's living room. His dancing in the title track introduced a new male movement vocabulary to Bollywood that choreographers have referenced ever since.

events.title: Taare Zameen Par Released
events.blurb: A film about an eight-year-old with undiagnosed dyslexia shipped off to boarding school for failing every subject — told largely from the child's hallucinatory perspective — earned ₹98 crore worldwide and prompted school boards across India to introduce dyslexia screening. Its child lead, discovered through an open casting call, had never acted before.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2007 — Aamir Khan's directorial debut, having taken over from Amole Gupte mid-production. Darsheel Safary, then 9, auditioned among 1,000 children. The film catalysed new Indian legislation on learning disability accommodation in schools. Khan dedicated the film to every child who had been misunderstood.

events.title: Baahubali: The Conclusion Released
events.blurb: The sequel to a Telugu fantasy epic that had left an entire nation debating one question — "Kattappa ne Baahubali ko kyun mara?" — opened to the largest advance booking in Indian cinema history, sold over 10 million tickets in its first weekend, and earned ₹1,000 crore net in India faster than any film before it, definitively crossing the barrier that only Hindi cinema had previously approached.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 2017 — directed by S.S. Rajamouli. The two-part production cost ₹430 crore, still the most expensive Indian film made at the time. The "why" answer to the Kattappa question — withheld for two years — turned its release into a cultural event rather than just a premiere.

events.title: Chauvet Cave Paintings
events.blurb: Deep inside a limestone gorge in southern France, artists of the Upper Paleolithic ventured hundreds of metres into darkness with torches of burning pine and painted more than 400 animals onto the walls — rhinos, horses, cave lions, mammoths — using charcoal and red ochre. The images show sophisticated techniques: perspective, shading, motion. They would remain sealed behind a rockslide until rediscovered by three cavers in 1994.
events.revealBlurb: c. 30,000 BCE — Chauvet-Pont-d'Arc, Ardèche. Radiocarbon dating of the charcoal remains controversial; estimates span 32,000-30,000 BCE. A meticulous replica opened to tourists in 2015; the original site is restricted to scientists to preserve a fragile microclimate.

events.title: Leonardo da Vinci Dies
events.blurb: A 67-year-old Florentine polymath died in a small château in the Loire Valley, where the French king had invited him to retire. On the easel beside his bed was an unfinished portrait of a Florentine merchant's wife that he had carried with him for sixteen years and never delivered to the man who had commissioned it. The king would acquire the painting from his executor; the subject's name, Lisa Gherardini, would eventually become the most famous name in art.
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 1519 — Leonardo at Clos Lucé, Amboise. The portrait is the Mona Lisa, now in the Louvre, which he had begun around 1503. He bequeathed his notebooks, which he wrote in mirror script, to his assistant Francesco Melzi.

events.title: Caravaggio's Calling of St Matthew
events.blurb: A 28-year-old painter completed the first of three monumental canvases for a chapel in a Roman church, depicting the moment when Christ walks into a tax collector's office and wordlessly summons a clerk to follow him. A shaft of natural light cuts diagonally across the scene, picking out faces from deep shadow. The painter used Roman street-people as models and dressed the apostles in contemporary clothes. The effect shocked and recruited a generation of imitators across Europe.
events.revealBlurb: 1600 — Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio, at the Contarelli Chapel, San Luigi dei Francesi. Art historians still argue about which figure is Matthew. The painter killed a man in a brawl six years later and died on the run at 38.

events.title: Hokusai's Great Wave
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Japanese printmaker produced the first of thirty-six woodblock prints depicting views of a sacred mountain, all showing it from different perspectives and in different weather. The first print, which viewers sometimes mistook for the title piece, showed an enormous wave curling in threatening foam over three small fishing boats, with the mountain a distant cone between its spray. The distinctive blue pigment, Prussian blue, was a recent European import.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1831 — Katsushika Hokusai. The print is one of the most widely reproduced images in the world; thousands of impressions survive. Hokusai called himself "the old man mad about drawing" and claimed he would become a true artist only at 110.

events.title: Duchamp's Fountain
events.blurb: A French artist submitted an ordinary porcelain urinal, signed with a pseudonym and dated, as a sculpture entitled "Fountain" to the first exhibition of New York's Society of Independent Artists. The Society's board — of which he was a member — voted after heated debate to reject it. He resigned in protest. The original object was lost; the artist authorized 17 replicas over subsequent decades, each now valued at millions.
events.revealBlurb: April 1917 — Marcel Duchamp, signed "R. Mutt 1917." The original was photographed by Alfred Stieglitz and then disappeared. A 2004 survey of 500 art-world professionals named it the most influential artwork of the 20th century. An artist attacked a replica with a hammer in 2006.

events.title: Battle of the Coral Sea
events.blurb: Two opposing fleets manoeuvred for days without either side's surface ships ever sighting the other, their aircraft flying hundreds of miles over open ocean to find and strike carriers whose decks they could not see. One navy lost a fleet carrier and the other lost a light carrier — but the strategic consequence was that an invasion convoy turned back.
events.revealBlurb: May 4–8, 1942 — the first naval battle in history fought entirely by aircraft. Neither fleet's ships came within sight of the other. Japan lost the light carrier Shōhō; the US lost USS Lexington. The two Japanese fleet carriers damaged at Coral Sea were then unavailable at Midway — a fact that proved decisive a month later.

events.title: Dieppe Raid
events.blurb: Roughly 6,000 troops — mostly Canadians — landed in daylight on a heavily defended beach overlooked by cliffs and were cut down before many could clear the waterline, suffering nearly 60 percent casualties in under ten hours. Planners later claimed the catastrophic failure provided lessons that saved countless lives in subsequent amphibious operations.
events.revealBlurb: August 19, 1942 — Operation Jubilee. Of 4,963 Canadians who embarked, only 2,210 returned to England; 907 were killed and 1,946 taken prisoner. The Germans, who had received advance intelligence, held their positions with minimal effort. Churchill admitted privately it was "a very heavy and grievous loss."

events.title: Battle of Leyte Gulf
events.blurb: Over four days, 282 warships clashed in four separate engagements across several hundred thousand square kilometres of open ocean — the largest naval battle in history by tonnage and personnel — as one navy committed virtually everything it had left to stop an invasion and the other deployed over 300 ships to press it through.
events.revealBlurb: October 23–26, 1944. Japan used its remaining fleet carriers as decoys with almost no aircraft aboard. A small force of US destroyers and escort carriers somehow bluffed a vastly superior Japanese battleship force into retreating at the Battle of Samar — one of the most improbable tactical reversals of the war. Japan also deployed kamikaze suicide aircraft in force for the first time.

events.title: Fall of Berlin
events.blurb: Soviet forces crossed into a capital city from three sides in a three-week assault involving two million soldiers, fighting block by block through a rubble-strewn metropolis defended by exhausted Wehrmacht troops, elderly home-guard units, and teenagers, while the city's absolute ruler retreated into an underground bunker and refused to concede that the war was lost.
events.revealBlurb: April 16 – May 2, 1945. Stalin had secretly put two Soviet army groups into a race for the Reichstag — willing to accept the extra casualties to ensure the symbolic prize fell to one particular commander. The famous "Victory Banner" was raised at 2:25 PM on April 30. German General Helmuth Weidling surrendered the city garrison on May 2 with fewer than 35,000 malnourished defenders left.

events.title: Death of Hitler
events.blurb: The dictator who had triggered the continent's most destructive conflict, directed the murder of millions, and sworn never to be taken alive shot himself in a subterranean command centre beneath a capital city now surrounded by enemy armies, having married his companion the previous day and designated a naval admiral as his successor.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1945 — Hitler shot himself at approximately 3:30 PM in the Führerbunker; Eva Braun took cyanide. Their bodies were carried to the garden and burned. By explicit prior order, no intact corpse was to fall into enemy hands. Soviet forces found the remains eight days after the surrender; Stalin kept the truth of their forensic identification secret for decades.
